claim: Working memory (WM) is the ability to actively hold information in memory over a delay period of seconds.
source: Working memory (WM), the ability to actively hold information in memory over a delay period of seconds, is a fundamental constituent of cognition.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific consensus about working memory.

claim: Working memory is a fundamental constituent of cognition.
source: Working memory (WM), the ability to actively hold information in memory over a delay period of seconds, is a fundamental constituent of cognition.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding and is cited in the introduction.

claim: Delay-period activity in sensory cortices has been observed in WM tasks.
source: Delay-period activity in sensory cortices has been observed in WM tasks, but whether and when the activity plays a functional role for memory maintenance remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: Whether and when delay-period activity in sensory cortices plays a functional role for memory maintenance remains unclear.
source: Delay-period activity in sensory cortices has been observed in WM tasks, but whether and when the activity plays a functional role for memory maintenance remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: AC neurons were active during the presentation of the auditory stimulus in the WM task.
source: Electrophysiological recordings revealed that AC neurons were active not only during the presentation of the auditory stimulus but also early in the delay period.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in the results section.

claim: AC neurons were active early in the delay period of the WM task.
source: Electrophysiological recordings revealed that AC neurons were active not only during the presentation of the auditory stimulus but also early in the delay period.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC during the stimulus epoch impaired WM performance.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC during the stimulus epoch and early delay period impaired WM performance, whereas suppression later in the delay period did not.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC during the early delay period impaired WM performance.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC during the stimulus epoch and early delay period impaired WM performance, whereas suppression later in the delay period did not.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC later in the delay period did not impair WM performance.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic suppression of neural activity in AC during the stimulus epoch and early delay period impaired WM performance, whereas suppression later in the delay period did not.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: AC is essential for information encoding in auditory WM task.
source: Thus, AC is essential for information encoding and maintenance in auditory WM task, especially during the early delay period.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the optogenetic suppression experiments during the stimulus epoch.

claim: AC is essential for information maintenance in auditory WM task, especially during the early delay period.
source: Thus, AC is essential for information encoding and maintenance in auditory WM task, especially during the early delay period.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the optogenetic suppression experiments during different delay periods.

claim: Working memory is a fundamental component of various cognitive functions.
source: It is a fundamental component of various cognitive functions (Baddeley, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baddeley, 1992.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is crucial for WM.
source: Previous studies have found that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is crucial for WM because sustained neural activity was observed in PFC during the delay period of WM task (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Meyers et al., 2012; Miller et al., 1996; Romo et al., 1999) and lesions to PFC produced profound WM deficits (Petrides, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sustained neural activity was observed in PFC during the delay period of WM task.
source: Previous studies have found that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is crucial for WM because sustained neural activity was observed in PFC during the delay period of WM task (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Meyers et al., 2012; Miller et al., 1996; Romo et al., 1999) and lesions to PFC produced profound WM deficits (Petrides, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Meyers et al., 2012; Miller et al., 1996; Romo et al., 1999.

claim: Lesions to PFC produced profound WM deficits.
source: Previous studies have found that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is crucial for WM because sustained neural activity was observed in PFC during the delay period of WM task (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Meyers et al., 2012; Miller et al., 1996; Romo et al., 1999) and lesions to PFC produced profound WM deficits (Petrides, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petrides, 2000.

claim: There is increasing evidence suggesting that sensory cortices are important components of the circuitry that underlies WM when the task requires short-term retention of sensory information.
source: Besides, there is increasing evidence suggesting that sensory cortices are important components of the circuitry that underlies WM when the task requires short-term retention of sensory information (Gayet et al., 2018; Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Scimeca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gayet et al., 2018; Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Scimeca et al., 2018.

claim: Human fMRI studies had been successful in decoding WM information from the activity of visual sensory cortices.
source: For example, human fMRI studies had been successful in decoding WM information from the activity of sensory cortices, both visual (Harrison and Tong, 2009; Serences et al., 2009) and auditory (Linke and Cusack, 2015; Linke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrison and Tong, 2009; Serences et al., 2009.

claim: Human fMRI studies had been successful in decoding WM information from the activity of auditory sensory cortices.
source: For example, human fMRI studies had been successful in decoding WM information from the activity of sensory cortices, both visual (Harrison and Tong, 2009; Serences et al., 2009) and auditory (Linke and Cusack, 2015; Linke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Linke and Cusack, 2015; Linke et al., 2011.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in visual sensory cortices.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in sensory cortices in visual (Supèr et al., 2001), auditory (Gottlieb et al., 1989), and somatosensory (Zhou and Fuster, 1996; Zhou and Fuster, 2000) modalities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Supèr et al., 2001.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in auditory sensory cortices.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in sensory cortices in visual (Supèr et al., 2001), auditory (Gottlieb et al., 1989), and somatosensory (Zhou and Fuster, 1996; Zhou and Fuster, 2000) modalities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gottlieb et al., 1989.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in somatosensory cortices.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys had observed memory-related activity during the delay period in sensory cortices in visual (Supèr et al., 2001), auditory (Gottlieb et al., 1989), and somatosensory (Zhou and Fuster, 1996; Zhou and Fuster, 2000) modalities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou and Fuster, 1996; Zhou and Fuster, 2000.

claim: The auditory cortex (AC) is known to be a major site for auditory information processing.
source: The auditory cortex (AC) is known to be a major site for auditory information processing.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of auditory cortex.

claim: AC neurons play a role in a number of auditory behavior tasks.
source: Some recent studies have reported that AC neurons also play a role in a number of auditory behavior tasks (Fritz et al., 2003; Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; Niwa et al., 2012; Otazu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fritz et al., 2003; Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; Niwa et al., 2012; Otazu et al., 2009.

claim: Correlates of auditory WM have been reported in AC.
source: Furthermore, correlates of auditory WM have been reported in AC (Bigelow et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bigelow et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2014.

claim: Traditional methods for perturbing neural activity such as surgical lesion, pharmacological inactivation, and tissue cooling techniques do not provide the temporal resolution required for delineating the functional role of AC in memory maintenance in WM task.
source: Traditional methods for perturbing neural activity such as surgical lesion, pharmacological inactivation, and tissue cooling techniques do not provide the temporal resolution required for delineating the functional role of AC in memory maintenance in WM task because they disrupt both the encoding of the sensory stimuli and their retention in WM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of traditional methods.

claim: Traditional perturbation methods disrupt both the encoding of the sensory stimuli and their retention in WM.
source: Traditional methods for perturbing neural activity such as surgical lesion, pharmacological inactivation, and tissue cooling techniques do not provide the temporal resolution required for delineating the functional role of AC in memory maintenance in WM task because they disrupt both the encoding of the sensory stimuli and their retention in WM.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how traditional methods work.

claim: Traditional perturbation methods could not be silenced rapidly enough to test when AC contributes to memory maintenance during the delay period.
source: Furthermore, the activity could not be silenced rapidly enough to test when AC contributes to memory maintenance during the delay period.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the temporal limitations of traditional methods.

claim: The behavioral performance in the auditory WM task declined with increasing duration of the delay period.
source: The behavioral performance declined with increasing duration of the delay period, indicating that the task required short-term memory processes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The decline in behavioral performance with increasing delay duration indicates that the task required short-term memory processes.
source: The behavioral performance declined with increasing duration of the delay period, indicating that the task required short-term memory processes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: A total of 915 neurons were recorded from AC during the auditory DMS task.
source: A total of 915 neurons were recorded, of which 287 (31.4%) exhibited activity related to the task (compared with baseline activity, evaluated with a paired t test, at the p<0.05 level) and were selected for further analysis.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data.

claim: 287 neurons (31.4% of recorded neurons) exhibited activity related to the task.
source: A total of 915 neurons were recorded, of which 287 (31.4%) exhibited activity related to the task (compared with baseline activity, evaluated with a paired t test, at the p<0.05 level) and were selected for further analysis.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the recorded neural data.

claim: More than 60% of AC neurons exhibited increased firing rate during the first 500 ms of the delay.
source: Figure 2c shows that more than 60% of AC neurons exhibited increased firing rate during the first 500 ms of the delay.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c based on analysis of neural recordings.

claim: The incidence of AC neurons with increased firing rate decreased to ~30% during 500–800 ms of the delay.
source: The incidence decreased to ~30% during 500–800 ms of the delay.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neural recordings shown in Figure 2c.

claim: For the majority of AC neurons (~90%), the elevated firing rate appeared in the first 800 ms of the delay period and did not persist any further.
source: For the majority of these units (~90%), the elevated firing rate appeared in the first 800 ms of the delay period and did not persist any further.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neural recordings.

claim: AC neurons carried the auditory information during the early delay period in WM task.
source: These results indicated that AC neurons carried the auditory information during the early delay period in WM task.
evidence: This is inferred from the ROC analysis showing stimulus selectivity during the early delay.

claim: 255 neurons responded to at least one auditory sample stimulus during passive presentation of the stimulus.
source: 255 neurons responded to at least one auditory sample stimulus (compared with baseline activity, paired t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of neural recordings during passive listening.

claim: In the passive presentation condition, AC neurons showed selectivity for a much shorter interval in the delay period compared to results obtained during WM task.
source: They showed selectivity for a much shorter interval in the delay period, in contrast to results obtained during WM task (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of neural recordings during WM task and passive listening shown in Figure 2.

claim: The continuation of neural activity into the delay period in WM task was not a passive process but was related to the animals' behavior.
source: These results indicated that the continuation of neural activity into the delay period in WM task was not a passive process but was related to the animals' behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between WM task and passive listening conditions.

claim: AC neurons exhibited elevated activity for 1000 ms from the stimulus onset, regardless of the duration of the sample stimulus.
source: Together with the result from the 200 ms sample stimulus duration task, which showed that the neurons continued to exhibit elevated activity for 800 ms into the delay period, all of these results showed that AC neurons exhibited elevated activity for 1000 ms from the stimulus onset, regardless of the duration of the sample stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments with different stimulus durations (200 ms, 300 ms, 400 ms).

claim: The temporal dynamics of the delay-period activity in AC might be relative to the stimulus onset rather than the offset.
source: These results suggested that the temporal dynamics of the delay-period activity in AC might be relative to the stimulus onset rather than the offset.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the stimulus duration experiments.

claim: Suppressing the activity of AC pyramidal neurons during the delay period caused a strong impairment in task performance (laser ON: 64.84 ± 1.59%; laser OFF: 77.98 ± 1.17%, n = 8, p=1.1 × 10−5).
source: Suppressing the activity of AC pyramidal neurons during the delay period caused a strong impairment in task performance (t-test, p=1.1 × 10−5, laser ON: 64.84 ± 1.59%; laser OFF: 77.98 ± 1.17%, n = 8), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=2.63 × 10−5, laser ON: 50.96 ± 2.65%; laser OFF: 31.66 ± 1.71%, n = 8) and a small decrease in hit rate (t-test, p=0.018, laser ON: 80.52 ± 1.74%; laser OFF: 87.69 ± 2.04%, n = 8) (Figure 3c, d).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Suppressing AC activity during the delay period resulted in a substantial increase in false alarm rate (laser ON: 50.96 ± 2.65%; laser OFF: 31.66 ± 1.71%, n = 8, p=2.63 × 10−5).
source: Suppressing the activity of AC pyramidal neurons during the delay period caused a strong impairment in task performance (t-test, p=1.1 × 10−5, laser ON: 64.84 ± 1.59%; laser OFF: 77.98 ± 1.17%, n = 8), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=2.63 × 10−5, laser ON: 50.96 ± 2.65%; laser OFF: 31.66 ± 1.71%, n = 8) and a small decrease in hit rate (t-test, p=0.018, laser ON: 80.52 ± 1.74%; laser OFF: 87.69 ± 2.04%, n = 8) (Figure 3c, d).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Suppressing AC activity during the delay period resulted in a small decrease in hit rate (laser ON: 80.52 ± 1.74%; laser OFF: 87.69 ± 2.04%, n = 8, p=0.018).
source: Suppressing the activity of AC pyramidal neurons during the delay period caused a strong impairment in task performance (t-test, p=1.1 × 10−5, laser ON: 64.84 ± 1.59%; laser OFF: 77.98 ± 1.17%, n = 8), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=2.63 × 10−5, laser ON: 50.96 ± 2.65%; laser OFF: 31.66 ± 1.71%, n = 8) and a small decrease in hit rate (t-test, p=0.018, laser ON: 80.52 ± 1.74%; laser OFF: 87.69 ± 2.04%, n = 8) (Figure 3c, d).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The delay-period activities of AC pyramidal neurons were important for maintaining the auditory information after the auditory stimulus ceased.
source: Thus, the delay-period activities of AC pyramidal neurons were important for maintaining the auditory information after the auditory stimulus ceased.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic suppression results during the delay period.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the stimulus epoch dramatically reduced the animals' ability to perform the task (laser ON: 61.71 ± 2.12%; laser OFF: 81.76 ± 1.3%, n = 9, p=4.92 × 10−7).
source: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the stimulus epoch dramatically reduced the animals' ability to perform the task (t-test, p=4.92 × 10−7, laser ON: 61.71 ± 2.12%; laser OFF: 81.76 ± 1.3%, n = 9), (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: AC was crucial for the initial encoding of auditory information in the WM task.
source: This result indicated that AC was crucial for the initial encoding of auditory information in the WM task.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic suppression during the stimulus epoch.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the delay period in a four tones auditory WM task resulted in substantial impairment in task performance (laser ON: 63.69 ± 2.58%; laser OFF: 73.48 ± 2.84%, n = 7, p=0.025).
source: Again, optogenetic suppression of AC during the delay period resulted in substantial impairment in task performance (t-test, p=0.025, laser ON: 63.69 ± 2.58%; laser OFF: 73.48 ± 2.84%, n = 7) (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments in a four tones task shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Optogenetic suppression during the epoch of 300–800 ms caused a strong reduction in behavioral performance (laser ON: 70.36 ± 2.5%; laser OFF: 80.51 ± 1.58%, n = 8, p=0.01).
source: Notably, optogenetic suppression during the epoch of 300–800 ms caused a strong reduction in behavioral performance (t-test, p=0.01, laser ON: 70.36 ± 2.5%; laser OFF: 80.51 ± 1.58%, n = 8) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Optogenetic suppression during the epoch of 800–1300 ms produced a smaller effect that was not significantly different from the laser-off condition (laser ON: 81.68 ± 1.72%; laser OFF: 83.91 ± 1.47%, n = 8, p=0.34).
source: Optogenetic suppression during the epoch of 800–1300 ms produced a smaller effect that was not significantly different from the laser-off condition (t-test, p=0.34, laser ON: 81.68 ± 1.72%; laser OFF: 83.91 ± 1.47%, n = 8) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Inactivation during 300–550 ms had an effect on behavioral performance (laser ON: 73.11 ± 2.23%, laser OFF: 79.38 ± 1.4%, n = 8, p=0.016).
source: Again, only inactivation during the 300–550 ms and 550–800 ms had an effect on behavioral performance (300–550 ms: t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 73.11 ± 2.23%, laser OFF: 79.38 ± 1.4%, n = 8; 550–800 ms: t-test, p<0.001, laser ON: 73.72 ± 2.82%, laser OFF: 86.31 ± 1.13%, n = 8), while the effect of inactivation after 800 ms was small and not statistically significant (800–1050 ms: t-test, p=0.38, laser ON: 77.93 ± 2%, laser OFF: 80.68 ± 2.25%, n = 7; 1050–1300 ms: t-test, p=0.42, laser ON: 84.97 ± 1.57%, laser OFF: 82.74 ± 2.19%, n = 8) (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4c-e.

claim: Inactivation during 550–800 ms had an effect on behavioral performance (laser ON: 73.72 ± 2.82%, laser OFF: 86.31 ± 1.13%, n = 8, p<0.001).

evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4c-e.

claim: The effect of inactivation during 800–1050 ms was small and not statistically significant (laser ON: 77.93 ± 2%, laser OFF: 80.68 ± 2.25%, n = 7, p=0.38).
source: Again, only inactivation during the 300–550 ms and 550–800 ms had an effect on behavioral performance (300–550 ms: t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 73.11 ± 2.23%, laser OFF: 79.38 ± 1.4%, n = 8; 550–800 ms: t-test, p<0.001, laser ON: 73.72 ± 2.82%, laser OFF: 86.31 ± 1.13%, n = 8), while the effect of inactivation after 800 ms was small and not statistically significant (800–1050 ms: t-test, p=0.38, laser ON: 77.93 ± 2%, laser OFF: 80.68 ± 2.25%, n = 7; 1050–1300 ms: t-test, p=0.42, laser ON: 84.97 ± 1.57%, laser OFF: 82.74 ± 2.19%, n = 8) (Figure 4c–e).

source: Again, only inactivation during the 300–550 ms and 550–800 ms had an effect on behavioral performance (300–550 ms: t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 73.11 ± 2.23%, laser OFF: 79.38 ± 1.4%, n = 8; 550–800 ms: t-test, p<0.001, laser ON: 73.72 ± 2.82%, laser OFF: 86.31 ± 1.13%, n = 8), while the effect of inactivation after 800 ms was small and not statistically significant (800–1050 ms: t-test, p=0.38, laser ON: 77.93 ± 2%, laser OFF: 80.68 ± 2.25%, n = 7; 1050–1300 ms: t-test, p=0.42, laser ON: 84.97 ± 1.57%, laser OFF: 82.74 ± 2.19%, n = 8) (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4c-e.

claim: AC is critical for WM only during the early delay period.
source: These results indicated that AC is critical for WM only during the early delay period.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal specificity of optogenetic suppression effects.

claim: In WM task with 3 s delay, perturbation during 300–800 ms had a significant disruption on behavior (laser ON: 71.69 ± 1.79%, laser OFF: 81.81 ± 1.73%, n = 8, p=1.16 × 10−3).
source: Again, only perturbation during 300–800 ms had a significant disruption on behavior (3 s delay, t-test, p=1.16 × 10−3, laser ON: 71.69 ± 1.79%, laser OFF: 81.81 ± 1.73%, n = 8; 7 s delay, t-test, p=0.033, laser ON: 72.8 ± 2.13%, laser OFF: 80.38 ± 2.32%, n = 7) (Figure 5a, c).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments with 3 s delay shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In WM task with 7 s delay, perturbation during 300–800 ms had a significant disruption on behavior (laser ON: 72.8 ± 2.13%, laser OFF: 80.38 ± 2.32%, n = 7, p=0.033).
source: Again, only perturbation during 300–800 ms had a significant disruption on behavior (3 s delay, t-test, p=1.16 × 10−3, laser ON: 71.69 ± 1.79%, laser OFF: 81.81 ± 1.73%, n = 8; 7 s delay, t-test, p=0.033, laser ON: 72.8 ± 2.13%, laser OFF: 80.38 ± 2.32%, n = 7) (Figure 5a, c).

claim: In WM task with 3 s delay, no obvious effects were seen when optogenetic suppression occurred after 800 ms (laser ON: 82.53 ± 1.92%, laser OFF: 85.33 ± 2.51%, n = 8, p=0.39).
source: No obvious effects were seen when optogenetic suppression occurred after 800 ms (3 s delay, t-test, p=0.39, laser ON: 82.53 ± 1.92%, laser OFF: 85.33 ± 2.51%, n = 8; 7 s delay, t-test, p=0.17, laser ON: 81.25 ± 1.83%, laser OFF: 84.69 ± 1.49%, n = 7) (Figure 5b, d).

claim: Mice could quickly adapt to the WM task with noise distractor, despite the initial drop in performance.
source: Mice could quickly adapt to the WM task with noise distractor, despite the initial drop in performance.
evidence: This is based on behavioral training data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: After 2 days of training, the performance on the third day of the WM task with noise distractor was no worse than that in the simple WM task (WM task with noise distractor: 79.55 ± 1.77%; simple WM task: 82.4 ± 1.58%, n = 9, p=0.247).
source: After 2 days of training, the performance on the third day of the WM task with noise distractor was no worse than that in the simple WM task (t-test, p=0.247, WM task with noise distractor: 79.55 ± 1.77%; simple WM task: 82.4 ± 1.58%, n = 9) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on behavioral training data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the early delay period after the distractor (500–800 ms) resulted in impairment in task performance (laser ON: 69.83 ± 2.8%; laser OFF: 77.32 ± 1.63%, n = 9, p=0.017).
source: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the early delay period after the distractor (500–800 ms) resulted in impairment in task performance (t-test, p=0.017, laser ON: 69.83 ± 2. 8%; laser OFF: 77.32 ± 1.63%, n = 9), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 45.6 ± 4.48%; laser OFF: 33.49 ± 2.5%, n = 9) and no significant change in hit rate (t-test, p=0.156, laser ON: 85.29 ± 1.68%; laser OFF: 88.41 ± 1.26%, n = 9) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments with distractor shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of AC after the distractor resulted in a substantial increase in false alarm rate (laser ON: 45.6 ± 4.48%; laser OFF: 33.49 ± 2.5%, n = 9, p=0.016).
source: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the early delay period after the distractor (500–800 ms) resulted in impairment in task performance (t-test, p=0.017, laser ON: 69.83 ± 2. 8%; laser OFF: 77.32 ± 1.63%, n = 9), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 45.6 ± 4.48%; laser OFF: 33.49 ± 2.5%, n = 9) and no significant change in hit rate (t-test, p=0.156, laser ON: 85.29 ± 1.68%; laser OFF: 88.41 ± 1.26%, n = 9) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments with distractor shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of AC after the distractor resulted in no significant change in hit rate (laser ON: 85.29 ± 1.68%; laser OFF: 88.41 ± 1.26%, n = 9, p=0.156).
source: Optogenetic suppression of AC during the early delay period after the distractor (500–800 ms) resulted in impairment in task performance (t-test, p=0.017, laser ON: 69.83 ± 2. 8%; laser OFF: 77.32 ± 1.63%, n = 9), with a substantial increase in false alarm rate (t-test, p=0.016, laser ON: 45.6 ± 4.48%; laser OFF: 33.49 ± 2.5%, n = 9) and no significant change in hit rate (t-test, p=0.156, laser ON: 85.29 ± 1.68%; laser OFF: 88.41 ± 1.26%, n = 9) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic suppression experiments with distractor shown in Figure 6b.

claim: AC activity is important for active early maintenance of the auditory information in the face of noise distractor in the WM task.
source: Thus, AC activity is important for active early maintenance of the auditory information in the face of noise distractor in the WM task.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic suppression experiments with distractor.

claim: Laser illumination during the delay period of a delayed go/no-go auditory discrimination task had no effect on the behavior (laser ON: 76.81 ± 2.01%, laser OFF: 79.9 ± 2.34%, n = 8, p=0.335).
source: We found that laser illumination had no effect on the behavior (t-test, p=0.335, laser ON: 76.81 ± 2.01%, laser OFF: 79.9 ± 2.34%, n = 8) (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments in delayed go/no-go task shown in Figure 7a.

claim: AC delay-period activity appeared to be more important in memory of the auditory cue but not the action plan.
source: Therefore, AC delay-period activity appeared to be more important in memory of the auditory cue but not the action plan.
